nameStory: The "forest tent caterpillar" gets its name from its woodland habitat and its close relationship to tent caterpillars. Ironically, despite the name, these caterpillars don't actually build the classic silk tents that their cousins do! Instead, they weave flat silky sheets on branches where they rest together during molting periods.
description: The Forest Tent Caterpillar Moth is a medium-sized brown moth that spends most of its visible life as a colorful, social caterpillar. The adult moths are typically brownish with subtle markings and appear in summer. The caterpillars are the stars of the show - they're blue with white diamond-shaped spots down their backs, yellow stripes along their sides, and can grow to about 2 inches long. These fuzzy caterpillars travel in groups along silk trails they lay down, creating quite a spectacle when they're abundant.

idTips.label: Caterpillar back pattern
idTips.description: Look for distinctive white diamond or keyhole-shaped spots running down the blue back - these feel slightly raised when you gently touch them and are unique among tent caterpillars

idTips.label: Group silk trails
idTips.description: Follow the shiny silk pathways on tree branches where groups travel together - these trails feel slightly sticky and have a faint sweet scent from pheromones

idTips.label: Fuzzy texture
idTips.description: The caterpillars have a soft, velvety feel with fine hairs that don't irritate skin when gently handled - much softer than they appear

idTips.label: No tent structures
idTips.description: Unlike Eastern Tent Caterpillars, these create flat silky mats on branches rather than baggy tent structures - the mats feel smooth and papery

idTips.label: Leaf damage pattern
idTips.description: Trees show characteristic defoliation where leaves are eaten from the outside edges inward, leaving behind brown, papery leaf veins that crackle when touched

habitat: Forest Tent Caterpillars thrive in deciduous woodlands throughout New England, particularly favoring areas with oak, sugar maple, aspen, and sweetgum trees. You'll find them from low-elevation forests to mid-elevation slopes, wherever these preferred host trees grow. They're especially common in mixed hardwood forests and woodland edges where sunlight creates good conditions for their host plants.

seasonality.spring: Eggs hatch in early spring and tiny caterpillars begin feeding on emerging leaves. This is when you'll first notice the characteristic group feeding behavior and silk trail formation.
seasonality.summer: Peak caterpillar activity occurs in early summer when they're largest and most noticeable. Adult moths emerge in mid to late summer and begin laying egg masses on twigs.
seasonality.fall: Adult moth activity winds down and winter egg masses become visible on bare twigs. The distinctive foam-covered egg clusters are easier to spot once leaves fall.
seasonality.winter: Only the winter egg masses are visible - look for gray, foam-like clusters wrapped around twigs that feel hard and cement-like to the touch.

funFact: Forest Tent Caterpillars have their own version of a highway system - they lay down silk trails containing chemical messages that tell other caterpillars which direction leads to the best food, creating insect traffic patterns that can stretch across entire trees!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with Eastern Tent Caterpillars, but Forest Tent Caterpillars have white diamonds down their backs (not a white stripe) and make flat silk mats instead of baggy tents. Memory trick: "Forest = Flat mats, Eastern = Enclosed tents."
contextualKnowledge: Despite their name suggesting they make tents, Forest Tent Caterpillars are the rebels of the tent caterpillar family - they never actually build tent-like structures. This naming confusion has led to many misidentifications, as people expect to find the characteristic silk tents that simply aren't there.
compareHints: Forest Tent Caterpillars differ from their close relative, the Eastern Tent Caterpillar, in several key ways: they have white diamond spots instead of a solid white stripe down the back, they make flat silk resting mats rather than enclosed tent structures, and they tend to feed higher in the forest canopy. The Eastern species typically builds obvious silk tents in tree crotches and has a more distinctive single white line down its back.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The closely related Forest Tent Caterpillar doesn't actually build tents despite its name, and has keyhole-shaped white markings instead of blue spots.
